Statements in a block run left to right. A law module is a file of edition 2. It holds provisions of law as data, with their notes and what the source says of them, each named by an address and covered by hashes; or, written by hand, it gives names to provisions and binds names to them. A .fr file is of one of two editions. A file of the first edition is a program of the language that Language describes, and carries no marker. A file of edition 2 is a law module: its first two significant tokens are the word edition and the integer 2; white space, line ends and comments before them

An address names a module, a provision or a note. It is / followed by one or more segments separated by /: Address = "/" Segment { "/" Segment } Segment = one or more of: ASCII letters, ASCII digits, "-", ".", "~" and the en dash U+2013 A segment is never empty, never . and never ... Two addresses a

A module with address A is the file layout::module_path(A) under its workspace's root: Each segment of the address maps to one path segment, character by character: Character of the address In the path a lower-case ASCII letter, a digit or ~ kept an upper-case ASCII letter _ followed by its lower-ca

The text of a law module is normalized. normalize::normalize normalizes a text in four steps: Put the text into Unicode Normalization Form C. Replace each of the 25 characters with the Unicode property White_Space with U+0020: U+0009 to U+000D, U+0020, U+0085, U+00A0, U+1680, U+2000 to U+200A, U+202

A module of law has one of three shapes: A unit holds one tree of provisions, whose top provision has the module's address. It also records the other addresses the source gives it (aliases), the container it stands in (within), the member of the source archive it was read from (source) and whether t

A provision has an address, a kind, a number, a heading and a status, each of the last three optional, and its items: text parts and child provisions, in document order. The address of a child lies below the address of its parent. The kind and the status are identifiers, such as section and repealed

A text is a list of runs: Run Holds words plain words link the linked words, and the target as the source writes it superscript superscript words subscript subscript words footnote marker the marker as shown, and the number of the footnote it points at The plain text of a text is the words of its ru

A note has an address, a layer, the group word of the source (ungrouped when there is none), its topics, an optional heading and blocks. The layer of a note is enacted or editorial. A note belongs to the unit or the container it is anchored in. A footnote belongs to its module. The footnotes of a mo

The text of a module falls into three layers: Layer Holds operative the provisions of a unit; the kind, number, heading, status and members of a container enacted the enacted notes editorial the source credit, the editorial notes, the footnotes and the footnote markers

In JSON the model has the form that serde derives: a struct is an object of its fields, an absent value is null, a variant without fields is its name in snake case (content, does_not_include), and any other variant is an object whose one key is its name in snake case. A text is {"runs": [...]}, and

A hash is 32 bytes of BLAKE3, written as 64 lower-case hexadecimal digits. Hash32 reads only that form: a text of another length, or one with an upper-case or any other character, is refused and the fault is named. Every hash is BLAKE3 over a sequence of frames. A frame is one tag byte, the length o

The tokens are those of the lexer of the first edition. Words such as module and content are identifiers that the parser compares by their text. A string is a JSON string literal. Line ends are not significant, and // begins a comment that runs to the end of its line. File = "edition" "2" Module ; M
